claims.claim: The efficiency gains from AI coding come with a trade‑off: teams face a higher burden of reviewing and integrating the new code.
claims.bestSource: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
claims.evidence: These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort.

The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm.

editorial.claim: The data also suggest that the extra code generated by AI does not automatically improve overall software output at the firm level.
Consequently, the overall productivity curve levels off, leaving the number of shipped applications unchanged.
These voices reinforce the idea that autonomous coding agents, while powerful, cannot replace the nuanced work of seasoned engineers.
Organizations should monitor how review processes adapt, as teams gain familiarity with the strengths and limits of these tools.
For now, the net effect on software delivery remains neutral, but the long‑term impact will depend on how teams evolve their workflows and tooling to manage the flood of code.
